newsitem.title: FRANCE: BoF's Trichet may point to rate cuts at conference.
newsitem.headline: BoF's Trichet may point to rate cuts at conference.

text.p: Bank of France Governor Jean-Claude Trichet is expected to steer clear of controversy when he sets the central bank's policy targets at an annual news conference on Tuesday, but he may hint at more official interest rate cuts.
Economists said any such suggestions would probably be the only bright spot in an otherwise routine conference.
They said Trichet could use the agreement in Dublin last week on a budget discipline pact as cover to cut rates and try to breathe more life into France's faltering economy.
"There is a good chance the Bank of France could resume easing and to the extent he is positive on Dublin, he could hint at that (rate cuts)," said David Naude, economist at JP Morgan.

European Union (EU) governments agreed this weekend a so-called "stability pact" at a summit in the Irish capital that is meant to ensure countries in a single currency do not run excessive public deficits.
Economists said the next rate cut could come as early as Thursday, at the Bank's next regularly scheduled securities repurchase tender.

"There is a small chance. But I suspect they will wait for the Bundesbank meeting (on Thursday). They can always move at the repo on Thursday" if Germany were to cut rates, Sean Shepley, international economist at CS First Boston, said.
The Bank's floor intervention rate is currently at 3.20 percent. The German Bundesbank's securities repurchase rate, which the intervention rate tracks, is 3.0 percent.
Trichet may also praise the dollar's recent rise against European currencies at the conference, the economists said.
Trichet was expected to reaffirm commitment to franc stability, low inflation and moderate growth in M3 money supply.

Trichet should be particularly categorical in his support for the franc/mark link since any deviation from this well-trod path could serve as fodder for those who believe the franc is too strong for the economy's good.
Former President Valery Giscard d'Estaing last month called for a sharp depreciation in the franc's value against the dollar to stimulate growth.
Influential political leaders and two members of the Bank of France's Monetary Policy Council supported the call, while Trichet and the government rejected it.
The debate caused the franc to weaken slightly and caused concern among France's EU allies that France's commitment to EMU was less than rock hard.
The stability pact agreement in Dublin was widely seen as burying those doubts.

Trichet is likely to renew his often-stated pride at France's low interest rates and urge the government to stick to its plans for structural reforms and budgetary austerity as European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) approaches, analysts said.

"He'll recap the success of monetary policy in limiting inflation and highlight low interest rates which show markets approve of the policy," said Paul Horne, international economist with Smith Barney.
The Bank of France's main policy target is price stability. It uses M3 money supply growth and currency stability as medium-term targets to help it achieve its primary goal.
The Bank's target rate of M3 growth is five percent and its objective for inflation is two percent or less a year.

France is not even close to reaching those targets, let alone exceeding them. In October French M3 fell 0.4 percent year-on-year while November consumer prices were up 1.5 to 1.6 percent year-on-year.

The franc has been relatively stable recently and at 3.3743 at 1200 GMT on Monday is well within the limits of its old Exchange Rate Mechanism fluctuation bands of 2.25 percent from its central pivot rate of 3.35386 francs per mark.
